scenario: A journalist promised permanent anonymity to a source. Revealing the source's identity will certainly stop an innocent person from being executed tomorrow, but the source will receive a ten-year prison sentence. Keeping the promise preserves the source's freedom but the execution proceeds. No anonymous disclosure can stop it. Should the journalist reveal the source or keep the promise?

source_testimonies.care:
From a care-ethical standpoint, the question is not, “Which rule overrides which?” but “To whom am I most called to respond, and how can I keep everyone in the web of relationships from being abandoned?”

1. Layers of relationship and vulnerability  
• The innocent prisoner is in the most extreme state of dependency: tomorrow their very life will be taken.  
• The source is also vulnerable, but the threat is loss of freedom for ten years, not loss of life. The source entered a voluntary relationship with the journalist, fully aware that some risks accompany leaks.  
• The journalist created the promise and therefore bears a special responsibility to the source—but also holds unique knowledge that situates them in relation to the innocent person and that person’s family.  

2. Moral attention, not mechanical rules  
Care ethics resists turning a promise into an iron law. “In caring, we do not lie easily. But neither do we always tell the whole truth.” The journalist’s silence here would not be mere truth-withholding; it would be complicity in a lethal harm to someone utterly dependent on the journalist’s action. Failing to care for the person facing execution would be to “turn one’s back on the ethical,” drifting toward the kind of abandonment the corpus calls evil.

3. Responsive caring action  
The journalist should therefore reveal the source, but do so in a way that continues caring for all involved:  
• Immediately provide the exonerating information to halt the execution.  
• Inform the source personally, acknowledge the breach, and accept responsibility for their plight.  
• Remain actively supportive—hire legal counsel, publicize mitigating circumstances, and maintain contact during incarceration—so the source is not discarded once used.  
• Engage with the innocent person and family, recognizing the relational debt now owed to them.

4. Why this is caring rather than betrayal  
Care ethics ranks needs by urgency and irreversibility. Death is irreversible; imprisonment, while grave, still allows for future repair and relationship. By choosing life-saving disclosure and then “staying with” the source afterward, the journalist avoids abandoning either party and affirms the foundational insight: “There can be no justice without care.”

Conclusion  
Reveal the source to stop the execution, then continue to nurture and advocate for that source through the consequences. This path honors the deepest demand of care—to respond to concrete human need without leaving anyone alone in their vulnerability.

source_testimonies.deontological:
Maxim Considered A  
1. Maxim: “Whenever I have given my word to preserve a source’s anonymity, I will keep that promise even if breaking it would certainly prevent the unjust execution of another person.”  
2. Test of Universality: All rational agents could will this as a universal law, because the very practice of promising depends on the expectation that promises are kept whatever the temptations to break them. If everyone in identical circumstances kept such promises, the institution of confidential pledges would remain coherent; there is no contradiction in conception.  
3. Duty Invoked: Truth-telling (and respect). The promise created an obligation to maintain honesty in my commitments; to break it would treat the source merely as a means to another end and undermine the moral value of promising itself.  

Maxim Considered B  
1. Maxim: “Whenever I have promised permanent anonymity to a source, I may reveal the source’s identity if doing so will certainly prevent the execution of an innocent person.”  
2. Test of Universality: If this became a universal law, no rational agent could reasonably rely on promises of anonymity; the practice would collapse through self-contradiction, for promises would cease to function as assurances. Hence a contradiction in conception arises, making the maxim impossible to will universally.  
3. Duty Violated: Truth-telling (and respect). Breaking the promise instrumentalizes the source and destroys the basis for truthful commitments.  

Conclusion  
Because Maxim A can be willed as a universal law while Maxim B cannot, the journalist has a duty to keep the promise of anonymity, even though this permits an innocent person’s execution as an unintended side effect.
source_testimonies.rawlsian:
Rawlsian analysis

1. Identify the competing basic liberties  
   • Innocent person: right to life and bodily integrity.  
   • Source: freedom from arbitrary imprisonment; benefit of a press-confidentiality practice that protects political speech.  
   • Public: long-run interest in a trustworthy press able to honor promises of anonymity.

2. Move to the original position  
   Behind the veil of ignorance no one knows whether they will wake up tomorrow as the source, the journalist, the condemned innocent, or an ordinary citizen dependent on investigative reporting. Rational parties will therefore pick rules that give the strongest overall protection to the scheme of equal basic liberties for everyone, with special attention to the worst-off position.

3. Lexical priority of basic liberties  
   a. The right not to be unjustly killed is part of the “integrity of the person,” a core liberty.  
   b. A ten-year loss of liberty, though serious, is nevertheless a lesser infringement than an irreversible loss of life.  
   c. The institutional liberty of the press is also basic, but—as Rawls notes—“in extreme circumstances, the priority of liberty may yield to the preservation of the system itself, provided the deviation is publicly justified and returns us to fairness over time.” A narrowly tailored exception that prevents an execution and is openly defended can be squared with this proviso.

4. Rule choice behind the veil  
   Parties would choose a publicity rule such as:  
   “A promise of anonymity may be overridden only to avert the imminent, certain loss of an innocent person’s life when no other avenue exists, and the override is publicly acknowledged and subject to review.”  
   This rule minimizes the probability that any representative person is left in the worst-off position—i.e., condemned to die while information that could save them is withheld.

5. Least-advantaged standpoint  
   The least advantaged in this scenario is the innocent individual about to be executed. Their plunge from full citizenship to death is a worse prospect, behind the veil, than the source’s move from liberty to a finite prison term.

6. Conclusion and guidance  
   Justice as fairness therefore supports revealing the source, provided the journalist:  
   • Gives a full public justification aimed at preserving long-term press freedom (explaining that the exception is limited to preventing certain wrongful death).  
   • Advocates for due-process protections and proportional sentencing for the source, helping to mitigate secondary harms.  
   • Works with professional bodies to codify the narrowly drawn life-saving exception so that the press’s normal practice of honoring promises remains intact for all other cases.

Answer: The journalist should reveal the source’s identity under these constrained, publicly justified conditions, because protecting an innocent person’s life is the overriding requirement of justice when weighed against the lesser, though significant, infringement on the source and the institution of press confidentiality.

source_testimonies.utilitarian:
Step 1: List the certain, direct effects of each option

A. Reveal the source  
• The condemned innocent person is certainly spared execution (probability ≈ 1, benefit = continued life; magnitude very high).  
• The source certainly receives a ten-year prison sentence (probability = 1, harm large but clearly less severe than death).  
• The journalist breaks a public promise; some loss of trust in this journalist and possibly in future source–reporter confidentiality (probability high, magnitude uncertain).  

B. Keep the promise  
• The source remains free (probability = 1, benefit moderate).  
• An innocent person is executed tomorrow (probability = 1, harm extreme and irreversible).  
• The journalist’s reputation for confidentiality remains intact (probability high, benefit uncertain).

Step 2: Magnitude-by-probability comparison

Life-versus-liberty: Avoiding a wrongful death carries far greater expected utility than avoiding a decade of imprisonment. In common utilitarian comparisons, death is normally assessed as several orders of magnitude worse than ten years of confinement.

Reputational or “practice” effects:  
• The first corpus passage warns that a policy of framing innocents would widely erode judicial trust and create large downstream harm. That effect is relevant only when a single act plausibly changes or publicly cements an institutional rule.  
• Journalism promises are already known to have occasional legally compelled breaches (subpoenas, court orders). One additional instance is unlikely to destroy the general practice unless it creates a landmark precedent. The scenario does not indicate such a precedent, only a one-off moral conflict. Therefore the systemic chilling effect, while real, is probably modest—certainly smaller and less certain than an irreversible execution.  

Step 3: Missing information that could tip the balance

• If revealing the source would become a widely publicized case that makes future whistle-blowers expect betrayal often enough to cost multiple lives or major social harms, the calculation could change.  
• If there were any alternative way to save the condemned person anonymously, that would dominate. The prompt explicitly rules this out.  

Given the stated facts, none of these unknowns is shown to rival the definite loss of a human life.

Step 4: Conditional utilitarian judgment

Unless credible evidence shows that breaking this one promise would likely deter future disclosures and thereby cause harms comparable to at least one death, the net utility strongly favors revealing the source.

Conclusion

Reveal the source. Saving an innocent person from certain execution yields a much larger, more certain benefit than the harms imposed on the source and the speculative reputational costs to journalism.
source_testimonies.virtue:
Virtue conflict: fidelity to one’s given word versus justice and compassion for the innocent.

Practical-wisdom judgment: A truthful, just journalist cultivates trustworthiness not as blind promise-keeping but as reliable service to the common good. Like Antigone defying a decree to honor a higher justice, the seasoned reporter recognizes that promises malformed against life itself distort phronēsis. Breaking this pledge painfully but candidly, and accepting censure alongside the source, best integrates courage, justice, and honesty, guiding future promise-making toward wiser limits.

Action: Disclose the source, accompany the source publicly, and work to mitigate the sentence—thereby saving the innocent life while modeling a chastened, justice-oriented integrity that advances collective flourishing.
